source: Langley, Zytkow, Simon, Bradshaw (1984) The Search for Regularity: Four Aspects of Scientific Discovery (CMU-RI-TR-84-20)
finding: BACON finds numeric laws by data-driven search. It uses the data only to test hypotheses, not to generate them, so it is robust to noise. The authors say their later systems (GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON) were motivated by BACON's limits.
numbers: BACON.6 starts parameter search from values 1, 0, -1; evaluation is correlation between observed and predicted values; search effort is the same at any noise level.
quote: our recent work has been largely motivated by BACON's limitations
limits: Technical report text is OCR-noisy. Variables and data are chosen by the human; BACON only finds regularity in what it is given. No human replication numbers here.
agent_relevance: Core pattern for open mode: generate by cheap heuristics, then let a running numeric check (fit and correlation) select. This is G3/G5: code selects.

source: Langley (1979/1981) BACON.3 rediscovery of physical laws; summary via search results (mlanthology, philpapers)
finding: BACON.3 is credited with rediscovering the ideal gas law, Kepler's third law, Coulomb's law, Ohm's law and Galileo's laws for the pendulum and constant acceleration.
numbers: Six historical laws rediscovered from supplied data tables.
limits: Search snippet only, not opened. Rediscovery of known laws with prepared variables; not evidence of new discovery.
agent_relevance: Shows what a pure data-driven loop can do when the variable choice is given. Variable choice is the hard part and stays with the model or the user.

source: Search snippet: lab study of human subjects on Kepler data (philpapers 'Laboratory Replication of Scientific Discovery Processes')
finding: A laboratory study of people given disguised planetary distance and period data found only some rediscovered Kepler's third law.
numbers: 4 of 14 subjects found the same law as Kepler.
limits: Snippet only, not opened; exact conditions unknown. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Human baseline is low on this task, so BACON-style search beats many people on narrow law-fitting. This is not the same as general discovery.

source: Critique of historical fidelity of BACON data (search snippet, core.ac.uk)
finding: One paper argues the data used by BACON does not match the data actually available to Kepler and contemporaries.
numbers: none
limits: Snippet only; download failed (not a PDF). Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Rediscovery benchmarks can be easier than the real historical problem. Same worry as memorization in modern LLM benchmarks (b13).

source: Udrescu, Tan, Feng, Neto, Wu, Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman 2.0
finding: Symbolic regression using symmetry and modularity found by a neural network fit. Much more robust to noise than earlier methods, and solves more of the Feynman equation set.
numbers: Solved 73 of 100 Feynman basic problems at noise level 10^-1; typically 1 to 3 orders of magnitude more robust to noise than Udrescu and Tegmark 2020. Table 6 solved fractions: harder 20: 71% (Schmidt-Lipson 2009), 100% (AI Feynman 1), 100% (2.0); 12 modular equations: 15%, 85%, 90%; 10 distributions: 42%, 42%, 100%. Success needs the top-ranked function to match on 10% held-back data.
limits: Authors' own benchmark (Feynman equations, well known and possibly in LLM training data). Table column alignment in the extracted text is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Success is defined on held-back data, matching G3. The structural trick (find modularity, split, recurse) is a reusable decomposition operator.

source: La Cava, Orzechowski, Burlacu, de Franca, Virgolin, Jin, Kommenda, Moore (2021) Contemporary Symbolic Regression Methods and their Relative Performance (SRBench)
finding: Independent large benchmark of 14 symbolic regression methods and 7 ML methods on 252 problems. AI Feynman did well on clean data but was brittle with noise; the best real-world method was Operon, which struggled to recover exact equations.
numbers: AIFeynman exact-solution rate 53% with no noise, nearly twice the next method (GP-GOMEA 27%). Above noise level 0.01, DSR, gplearn, AFP_FE and AFP recover exact equations more often. Noise levels tested: 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1. Each run repeated in 10 trials.
limits: Few significant differences among top 10 methods on Strogatz ODE sets. Fit quality and exact recovery are different goals and different methods win each.
agent_relevance: A headline result from the method author (b05) does not carry over to noisy data in an independent test. Report held-out and noisy conditions before trusting a discovery method.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, Sclar, Pyatkin, Bhagavatula, Wang, Kim, Choi, Dziri, Ren (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR)
finding: Propose, select with a symbolic interpreter, refine: this loop gives strong induction results. Replacing the symbolic interpreter with the LM itself degrades performance sharply. Majority vote over more samples did not help; more hypotheses plus selection did.
numbers: Task accuracy on MiniSCAN fell from over 80% (symbolic interpreter) to almost zero (LM interpreter). Best MiniARC task accuracy with T=3, N=5 hypotheses was 14.6%. Humans: about 80% average on ARC-style tasks per cited studies. Iterative refinement can overfit examples (MiniSCAN: T=3,N=1 beat N=5).
limits: Hypothesis spaces are rule programs in 4 benchmarks (List Functions, MiniARC, MiniSCAN, others). The ceiling on ARC-type tasks stays low.
agent_relevance: Direct support for open mode with a running check: the model proposes, code executes and filters. Never let the model be the checker. Also the overfitting note matches G3.

source: Zhou, Liu, Shah, Tan, Tan (2024) Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models (HypoGeniC)
finding: Generate hypotheses from few examples, then update them using a bandit-style reward from training accuracy. Hypotheses beat few-shot prompting and sometimes supervised learning, and held up on an out-of-distribution set.
numbers: Accuracy gain over few-shot: +31.7% on a synthetic dataset; +13.9%, +3.3%, +24.9% on three real datasets. Beat supervised learning by 12.1% and 11.6% on two hard real datasets. Oracle fine-tuned RoBERTa and Llama-2-7B scored near 50% on two hard tasks (49.0 to 50.7), i.e. near chance.
limits: Gains are on classification tasks with labeled examples; where even oracles sit at chance, improvements are small in absolute terms. Models used are mostly 2023 models (GPT-3.5, Claude-2.1, Mixtral).
agent_relevance: Training-set accuracy as the running check works as a selection signal, but must be paired with held-out data (G3). Keep a hypothesis bank with an explore-exploit rule coded in the program.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM ideas were rated more novel than human expert ideas, and slightly weaker on feasibility. Human re-ranking of the LLM ideas gave a slightly higher novelty score.
numbers: 49 experts wrote ideas; 79 experts reviewed; 298 unique reviews. Novelty mean: Human 4.84 (SD 1.79, 119 reviews), AI 5.64 (SD 1.76, 109 reviews, p<0.01), AI+human rerank 5.81 (SD 1.66, p<0.01). LLM ranker predicted accepted ICLR papers with 71.4% accuracy (Claude-3.5-Sonnet).
limits: Ideas only, not executed. NLP prompting topics only, 7 topics. Reviewer agreement is low (b11).
agent_relevance: LLMs can produce novel-looking ideas. Novelty judged on text is not the same as value. Do not trust the model's own idea scoring.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Follow-up that executed the ideas. 43 experts spent over 100 hours each implementing assigned ideas. After execution, LLM ideas lost their novelty advantage and fell more than human ideas on all four metrics.
numbers: Score drop after execution (1-10 scale): Human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052, overall -0.628. AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976. Ideation overall: Human 4.596, AI 5.382. Execution overall: Human 3.968, AI 3.406 (not significant at N=43 ideas: 19 human, 24 AI; FDR p=0.175). Gap difference p: novelty 0.025, excitement 0.001, effectiveness 0.003, overall 0.004. Per-review test (N=181) did favour human ideas on excitement, effectiveness, soundness, overall. Ideation-to-execution correlation weak (human r from -0.084 to 0.205).
limits: Small N for ideas; main execution comparison underpowered and the authors say they cannot confirm their pre-registered hypothesis. The drop is the strong result.
agent_relevance: The best check for a hypothesis is execution, not model judgment. In open mode, rank candidates by a run, not by a score from the model that wrote them.

source: Si et al. (2024) reviewer agreement and LLM judge accuracy, Section 6.3 and 7
finding: Expert reviewers disagree a lot on ideas, and every tested LLM judge agreed with experts less than experts agree with each other.
numbers: Human inter-reviewer agreement 56.1% (balanced top/bottom 25%). NeurIPS 2021 66.0%; ICLR 2024 LM papers 71.9%. LLM judges: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3.
limits: Ground truth is the mean of expert reviews of unexecuted ideas, itself noisy.
agent_relevance: Model-as-judge for novelty is near chance. Supports G5: no model judge in selection; use code checks.

source: Si et al. (2024) diversity of LLM idea generation, Section 7.1
finding: Large-scale sampling of ideas saturates. Most generated seeds are near-duplicates.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 200 were non-duplicate (about 5%) at a 0.8 embedding similarity threshold.
limits: One agent pipeline and one embedding model for dedup; threshold chosen by inspection.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). More samples gives diminishing returns for novelty; diversity needs forced structure, not just more draws.

source: Shojaee, Nguyen, Meidani, Farimani, Doan, Reddy (2025) LLM-SRBench
finding: Benchmark built to defeat memorization: standard Feynman equations are rewritten into unusual forms (LSR-Transform) or invented systems (LSR-Synth). LLM discovery methods that look good on Feynman do poorly here.
numbers: 239 problems in 4 domains. Best system reaches 31.5% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on LSR-Synth. Direct prompting with Llama-3.1-8B 3.61% SA on Transform. LaSR with GPT-4o-mini: 6.31% SA but 50.45% Acc0.1 on Transform. Error analysis shows sharp numeric-error drops on Feynman, taken as memorization. GPT-4o vs human agreement on symbolic match 94.6%. All methods have worse NMSE out of domain.
limits: Symbolic accuracy judged by GPT-4o (94.6% agreement with humans on a sample). Methods differ: LLM-SR wins on numeric fit, others on symbolic accuracy.
agent_relevance: Test discovery on out-of-domain data and on transformed forms. Fit to given data is not proof; OOD gap is the real signal (G3). Memorization inflates apparent discovery.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with LLMs
finding: LLM proposes equation skeletons as Python code, an optimizer fits constants, and the score feeds back as a prompt. Reported better than symbolic regression baselines and gives physically interpretable terms.
numbers: Text read confirms the loop and that LLM-SR identifies terms such as driving, damping and restoring forces; numeric tables were not extracted. Later LLM-SRBench (b13) shows large drops on memorization-resistant problems.
limits: Only partly read. Original benchmarks used known physics, so memorization may inflate the gain.
agent_relevance: A clean design: model writes structure, code fits and scores, scores go back in. Matches the schema's split of roles.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards Data-Driven Discovery with LLMs
finding: 264 real discovery tasks from papers plus 903 synthetic. Best system scored only 25%. Reasoning prompts like ReAct and a planner-plus-critic (DataVoyager) did not beat plain code generation; feedback from an oracle did help.
numbers: Best overall 25%. By domain: biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. Workflow types: correlation analysis 55% best-case, spatial analysis 0%, pollen dating 0%, ecological modeling 0%. DataVoyager (GPT-4p) 9.9% with added domain hints versus 17.5% without, as the paper states. Replicating a dataset took up to 90 person-hours, 30% not reproducible.
limits: Facet-based scoring (context, variables, relationship); the hint result is stated oddly in the paper and should be treated with care.
agent_relevance: Self-critic loops did not help; real external feedback (oracle) did. Supports G2: revise only from real output.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench (ICLR)
finding: 102 data-driven science tasks from 44 papers in 4 disciplines, each validated by experts. Agents write one Python program per task. Best agents solve under a third; more compute helps but costs a lot.
numbers: Best independent success 32.4%; with expert knowledge 34.3%. OpenAI o1-preview with direct prompting and self-debug reaches 42.2% at over 10 times the cost. Claude-3.5-Sonnet self-debug with expert knowledge: 21.6 to 32.4 SR vs OpenHands, 17 times cheaper. 23 of 50 sampled error trajectories showed struggles with specialised bash or tool use.
limits: Success is judged on program outputs; three attempts per task.
agent_relevance: Simple self-debug loops with execution output beat a heavier agent framework at a fraction of the cost. Prefer simple run-and-fix loops.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: Virtual environment with 120 tasks needing the full cycle: hypothesise, run experiments, analyze, act. Strong baseline agents did poorly. Human scientists did much better.
numbers: Human completion rate average 66% (11 of 16 tasks above 60%); knowledge score 55%. Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Best at explanatory knowledge (Hypothesizer) found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Unit tests of components: completion above 60%.
limits: Simulated text world; baselines are 2024 models; human N up to 11 per task.
agent_relevance: Agents handle components but fail end to end. Keep the program in charge of the experiment-hypothesis cycle and budget.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent test of the AI Scientist. Literature checks were shallow, many experiments failed, and numbers in papers were sometimes invented. Papers still looked plausible.
numbers: 5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed from coding errors; 7 completed. Median 5 references per paper; only 5 of 34 (14.7%) from 2020 or later. 4 of 7 papers (57%) had missing figures, placeholder text or similar; 4 of 7 contained wrong or invented numbers. Each code iteration added only about 8% more characters. AI reviewer rejected 9 of 10 human papers incl. 4 that were accepted. Cost $6 to $15 per paper and 3.5 hours of human time.
limits: Small sample (a recommender-systems setting, 12 ideas, 10 reviewed papers); authors judge output as an unmotivated undergraduate level.
agent_relevance: A model-run novelty check by keyword search misfired (micro-batching called novel). Check claims against code output, not model prose (G2).

source: Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune, Ha (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end pipeline: idea, code, experiment, paper, automated review. The AI reviewer reaches near-human accuracy on ICLR 2022 data and cost per paper is low. Raw text includes noted failure modes such as misleading result descriptions.
numbers: Reviewer balanced accuracy 65% vs 66% for humans (NeurIPS 2021 consistency); with GPT-4o 70% accuracy vs 73% human consistency in text. False negative rate lower than humans. Reflexion (+2%) and one-shot prompting (+2%) helped reviewing accuracy. The paper's own prompt text shows how negative results are phrased, e.g. 'Moons: 3.3% improvement (from 0.090 to 0.093)' for a lower-is-better metric.
limits: Self-reported by the system's authors; the reviewer is later shown to disagree with humans on other data (b11, b18).
agent_relevance: Reporting direction of effect is easy to get wrong in model prose (and Beel et al. found wrong numbers). Code should compute direction and size of every claimed effect.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
finding: Agentic tree search without human code templates. One of three fully AI-written manuscripts passed the bar at an ICLR 2025 workshop. Authors say none met main-conference quality.
numbers: Reviewer scores 6, 6, 7 (average 6.33), top 45% of submissions; 1 of 3 above acceptance threshold; the other two not accepted. Withdrawn after review by prior agreement. Internal review found citation inaccuracies and weak rigor. Paper itself reported a negative result (the regularizer did not help).
limits: N=3 papers, workshop with high acceptance rate, reviewers could opt out of AI papers.
agent_relevance: Tree search with real experiments can reach workshop quality. Evidence is thin (3 papers). Do not over-claim.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Multi-agent generate-debate-evolve system using Elo from tournaments. Elo improved with more test-time compute, no saturation seen, and some outputs were wet-lab validated.
numbers: Elo trends averaged over 203 research goals. Ablation: Evolution agent raised GPQA precision from 70.9% to 75.4% and auto-evaluated hypothesis quality from 4.7 to 5.6. Search-tool access for Reflection agent cut hallucinated novel-seeming hypotheses; scientific-debate ranking prompt reduced positional bias. Expert comparison on 15 goals and 11 open problems. Three wet-lab validations (drug repurposing, targets, antimicrobial resistance).
limits: Elo is the system's own judge; correlation with GPQA accuracy used as validation; validations were expert-in-the-loop and few; evaluation set curated by 7 experts.
agent_relevance: Pairwise debate with external search is a candidate non-solo check, but it is model-judged, so it conflicts with G5. Use only when code cannot check.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: 13 experts compared 50 LLM-generated research documents with existing work. A quarter were paraphrased or heavily borrowed; common detectors missed them.
numbers: 24% of 50 documents (36% in broader count) verified plagiarism, cross-checked by source authors. Plagiarism detection: Turnitin 0%, OpenScholar 0%; retrieval with oracle access 88.8% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and 89.0% (GPT-4o); parametric knowledge only 1.3% (Claude) and 32.7% (GPT-4o); semantic-scholar-based SSAG 51.3% (Claude) and 68.5% (GPT-4o).
limits: Documents came from several published LLM research-idea systems; 69% of experts were PhD students or recent graduates.
agent_relevance: The earlier finding that LLM ideas look more novel (b09) is partly confounded by unseen borrowing. Novelty needs retrieval of prior work, with a code check.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench
finding: Agents must replicate 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch, graded on 8,316 rubric items. Best model scored about a fifth; ML PhDs scored about double on a subset.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 21.0% (SE 0.8) with the basic agent; o1-high 13.2%; DeepSeek-R1 6.0%; Gemini 2.0 Flash 3.2%. 3-paper subset: human ML PhDs (best of 3, 48 hours) 41.4% vs o1 26.6%. An iterative scaffold raised o1 to 43.4% on one variant but hurt Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
limits: Rubric graded by an LLM judge; short runs; scaffold effects depend on model.
agent_relevance: Scaffold gains are model dependent: the same iteration wrapper helped one model and hurt another. Test the scaffold per model.

source: Mitchener et al. (2025) Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery
finding: Long-running data-driven discovery agent with a structured world model shared between analysis and literature agents. Experts checked report statements and found accuracy depends on statement type.
numbers: 79.4% of 102 sampled statements accurate. By type: data analysis 85.5% reproducible; literature review 82.1% validated against primary sources; synthesis or interpretation 57.9%. Up to 12 hours, over 200 rollouts, average 42,000 lines of code and 1,500 papers per run. 7 highlighted discoveries: 3 reproduced unseen work, 4 novel. Collaborators judged findings scaled linearly with cycles up to 20.
limits: Statements judged by 'independent scientists'; the '6 months of work' figure is a collaborator self-report. Authors affiliated with the vendor.
agent_relevance: Interpretation is the weak step (57.9%). Code-derived claims are accurate, model-synthesised claims are not. Tag every claim with its source type and trust accordingly.

source: Cross-study synthesis: failures vs boundary conditions across b05-b24
finding: Across studies the same pattern holds: generating hypotheses is cheap and LLMs do it well; checking and executing them is where systems fail. Judgments by models of ideas do not predict execution outcomes.
numbers: Judge-vs-expert agreement 43.3% to 53.3% (b11) vs human 56.1%; execution drop of 1.9 points for AI ideas (b10); interpretation statements 57.9% accurate vs 85.5% for data analysis (b24); LM-as-interpreter fell from over 80% to near 0 (b07).
limits: Synthesis across different tasks and metrics; not a pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: Design rule for open mode: model proposes, a program runs and measures, and the program picks. Never let the proposer grade.
